'''Zsuzsanna Izsvák''' (born 18 August 1961<ref>''"Million Euro Award to Young Hungarian Scientist at the MDC Research on “Mobile Genetic Elements” - High biomedical Potential"'', [https://www.mdc-berlin.de/news/archive/2004/20040826-million_euro_award_to_young_hungarian_scie  Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine (MDC) press release], 26 August 2004.</ref>) is a [[Hungary|Hungarian]]-[[Germany|German]] geneticist and biologist. She obtained the Candidate of Biological Sciences degree in 1993 and the Doctor of Biological Sciences in 2011. She was elected as a corresponding (external) member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] in 2019.<ref>CV of Zsuzsanna Izsvák, [https://www.mdc-berlin.de/content/group-leader?mdcbl%5B0%5D=/izsvak%23t-profile&mdctl=0&mdcou=20753&mdcot=1&mdcbv=62qerrvZYudLa1rxTezzayKRWaPUAUaO_p8MZOJsRDg Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine (MDC) website], retrieved 4 November 2025.</ref>

==Career and scientific work==

From 1984 to 1991 she worked at the [[Biological Research Centre (Hungarian Academy of Sciences)|Biological Research Centre]] of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] in [[Szeged]]. She received her MSc in biology from the Faculty of Science at [[University of Debrecen|Kossuth Lajos University Debrecen]] in 1987.

Between 1991 and 1997 she worked in the [[United States of America|United States]] at the [[University of Minnesota]]. In 1999 she moved to the [[Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association|Max Delbrück Centre for Molecular Medicine (MDC)]] in [[Berlin]], where she has led the “Mobile DNA” research group since 2004.<ref>Mobile DNA research group homepage, [https://www.mdc-berlin.de/izsvak Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine (MDC) website], retrieved 4 November 2025.</ref> Between 2009 and 2011 she held a guest professorship at the [[University of Debrecen]].

Her main research field is unstable segments of the genome (mobile genetic elements). Alongside her husband Zoltán Ivics she reconstructed an extinct [[Transposable element|transposon]] system in vertebrates, which they named “[[Sleeping Beauty transposon system|Sleeping Beauty]]”. They also discovered a human-specific transposon-based regulatory system in stem cells. These contributions have been regarded as an international breakthrough in molecular genetics, stem-cell research, genetic engineering and medical therapy.<ref>''“Sleeping Beauty” – Molecule of the Year'', [https://www.mdc-berlin.de/news/archive/2010/20100119-_sleeping_beauty____molecule_of_the_year Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine (MDC) press release], 19 January 2010.</ref>

==Major awards and honours==

* European Young Investigator Award (EURYI), 2004, awarded for research on mobile genetic elements.<ref>''Project descriptions of the EURYI award winners'', [http://archives.esf.org/coordinating-research/euryi/awards/2004.html EURYI website], retrieved 4 November 2025.</ref>
* Molecule of the Year Award, 2009, in recognition of the “Sleeping Beauty” transposon work.<ref>''“Sleeping Beauty” – Molecule of the Year'', [https://www.mdc-berlin.de/news/archive/2010/20100119-_sleeping_beauty____molecule_of_the_year Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine (MDC) press release], 19 January 2010.</ref>
